source.title_on_document: Scaffolding Creativity or Homogenizing Outputs?: GPT-based Virtual TA's Impact on Student Ideation in Graduate Education

supplement.holds: The paper refers to Shah et al. (2024) for the prompts students used; it mentions no supplementary material or appendix.

paper_design_summary: Cohort comparison in one graduate course on video games at the University of Pennsylvania: the 2023 cohort (N=20) wrote a Minecraft play journal without JeepyTA, and the 2024 cohort (N=22) wrote the same assignment with access to JeepyTA, a GPT-3.5 discussion-forum teaching assistant. Two coders counted each student's ideas for educational uses of Minecraft and classed them as trivial, promising, or fully formed; ANCOVAs compare cohorts. Within the 2024 cohort, a descriptive thematic analysis compares JeepyTA-driven with student-driven ideas, including theme repetition across students.

studies.label: 2023 vs 2024 cohort comparison (Minecraft play journal ideas)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to JeepyTA came with course year: the 2024 cohort had it, the 2023 cohort did not.
assignment.quote: this paper addresses the following research questions using data from a 2023 cohort acting as the control group (without JeepyTA) and a 2024 cohort acting as the treatment group (with JeepyTA)
assignment.locator: p. 2, Study Purpose and Research Questions; p. 12 names self-selection bias as a limitation

arms.name: 2023 (Control)
arms.description: 2023 cohort; play journal written without JeepyTA

arms.name: 2024 (JeepyTA)
arms.description: 2024 cohort; play journal written with access to JeepyTA in the course discussion forum

participants.who: Graduate students in the course 'Video Games and Virtual Worlds as Sites for Learning and Engagement' (Graduate School of Education, University of Pennsylvania), spring 2023 and spring 2024 cohorts
participants.quote: A total of 42 play journals were collected from participants in the 2023 (without JeepyTA) cohort (N=20) and the 2024 (with JeepyTA) cohort (N=22).

ai_tool.name_model: JeepyTA, built on OpenAI GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613), customized with course materials
ai_tool.how_used: Integrated into the course discussion forum; students were urged to 'thought-partner' with JeepyTA about educational applications of Minecraft, with no specific requirements for how to use its recommendations (pp. 3-4).

task.description: Play journal assignment proposing educational applications of Minecraft; only the sections describing educational applications were coded.

outcomes.name: Fully formed (FF) ideas per student
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Per-student count of ideas manually classified as fully formed: comprehensive and detailed ideas with concrete examples of real-life application, game mechanics, and domain knowledge (p. 5, Table 1). Two coders independently coded all journals and resolved differences through social moderation (p. 7, Coding the data). The cohort ANCOVA controlled for total ideas; a follow-up also controlled for prior Minecraft experience (p. 7, Data Analysis; pp. 8-9, Table 3 and Fully Formed Ideas).

contrasts.reported: Fully formed (FF): 2023 (Control) N=20, count 7, mean 0.35 (SD 0.49); 2024 (JeepyTA) N=22, count 18, mean 0.82 (SD 0.96). ANCOVA cohort effect controlling for total ideas F(1, 39) = 4.652, p = 0.037; controlling for total ideas and Minecraft experience F(1, 39) = 4.83, p = 0.034.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Tables 2 and 3; p. 9, Fully Formed Ideas

contrasts.reported: Total Ideas: 2023 (Control) N=20, count 48, mean 2.40 (SD 1.43); 2024 (JeepyTA) N=22, count 67, mean 3.05 (SD 2.3). No test of the cohort difference in total ideas is reported; total ideas enters the ANCOVAs as a covariate.

outcomes.name: Theme repetition across students: JeepyTA-driven vs student-driven ideas (2024 cohort only)
outcomes.question: across_people

contrasts.reported: Within 2024 only (no 2023 comparison): JeepyTA-driven ideation 50 ideas from 18 students (36 trivial, 8 promising, 6 FF); student-driven 17 ideas from 10 students (2 trivial, 3 promising, 12 FF). Most frequent JeepyTA-driven themes: 'Teamwork and collaboration' (10 students), 'Creativity with storytelling' (8), 'Virtual field trips' (6); most frequent student-driven themes: architecture (3 students), math (2). 'Because of the small sample size, no statistical tests were conducted.' The p. 11 text gives student-driven as '12 FF; 3 promising; 5 trivial', against 2 trivial in Table 4.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Table 4; p. 11, Homogeneity of ideas

diversity_detail.metric: Manually coded frequencies of idea themes across students, comparing JeepyTA-driven with student-driven ideation; descriptive thematic overlap, with no normalized diversity index (p. 11, Homogeneity of ideas).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Student journal ideas within the 2024 cohort: 50 JeepyTA-driven ideas from 18 students versus 17 student-driven ideas from 10 students. Theme frequencies count students whose responses included each theme. No 2023 cohort diversity comparison is reported (pp. 10-11, Table 4 and Homogeneity of ideas).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Descriptive only. The authors state that no statistical tests were conducted because of the small sample size; no standard error or confidence interval for thematic diversity is reported (p. 11, RQ3(a) continuation and Homogeneity of ideas).
diversity_detail.notes: The students contributing to the two idea-origin categories overlap and must not be added to obtain a participant count; both categories belong to the same 2024 cohort of 22 students (p. 4, Data Source; p. 10, Table 4 and following paragraph). These categories were coded from the journals, not separately assigned groups. Student-driven ideas could receive elaboration from JeepyTA (p. 7, Table 1 continuation). Direction is coded as lower diversity for JeepyTA-driven ideas, based on greater repetition of themes. The reported theme frequencies are descriptive counts and do not supply any of the effect-summary formats listed in statistics_available. The source discrepancy in student-driven trivial ideas is retained in reported: 2 in Table 4 and its p. 10 narrative, but 5 in the p. 11 narrative.

outcomes.name: Promising ideas per student
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Per-student count of manually classified ideas. Promising ideas show potential and more detail than trivial ideas but require further development; they describe aspects of real-life application, game mechanics, and domain knowledge while lacking concrete examples (p. 5, Table 1). Two coders independently coded all journals and resolved differences through social moderation (p. 7, Coding the data). The cohort ANCOVA controlled for total ideas; a follow-up also controlled for prior Minecraft experience (p. 7, Data Analysis). These are idea counts within the existing cohorts, not additional participants.

contrasts.reported: Promising: 2023 (Control) N=20, count 17, mean 0.85 (SD 0.93); 2024 (JeepyTA) N=22, count 11, mean 0.50 (SD 1.06). ANCOVA cohort effect controlling for total ideas F(1, 39) = 2.504, p = 0.122; controlling for total ideas and Minecraft experience F(1, 39) = 4.5, p = 0.041. The unadjusted mean is lower in 2024, but the p. 9 narrative describes the effect after also controlling for Minecraft experience as a larger number of promising ideas in 2024. Adjusted means and signed coefficients are not reported; direction is coded mixed to retain both the unadjusted result and the adjusted narrative.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Tables 2 and 3; p. 9, Promising Ideas (including degrees of freedom and adjusted-direction statement)

outcomes.name: Trivial ideas per student
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Per-student count of manually classified ideas. Trivial ideas are superficial, lack depth and concrete examples, and offer little or no detail about real-life application, game mechanics, or domain knowledge (p. 5, Table 1). Higher counts reflect more superficial ideas. Two coders independently coded all journals and resolved differences through social moderation (p. 7, Coding the data). The cohort ANCOVA controlled for total ideas; a follow-up also controlled for prior Minecraft experience (p. 7, Data Analysis). These are idea counts within the existing cohorts, not additional participants.

contrasts.reported: Trivial: 2023 (Control) N=20, count 24, mean 1.20 (SD 1.36); 2024 (JeepyTA) N=22, count 38, mean 1.73 (SD 2.53). ANCOVA cohort effect controlling for total ideas F(1, 39) = 0.019, p = 0.891; controlling for total ideas and Minecraft experience F(1, 39) = 0.011, p = 0.917. The unadjusted mean is higher in 2024; neither ANCOVA reports a significant cohort effect.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 2; p. 9, Table 3 continuation; pp. 9-10, Trivial Ideas (including degrees of freedom)

The exact number of overlapping participants is not reported.

company_involvement.description: Coauthor Mamta Shah lists Elsevier as an affiliation, alongside the Graduate School of Education, University of Pennsylvania. Company involvement is recorded on this affiliation basis; the manuscript does not state company sponsorship or funding.

eligibility.reason: Access to JeepyTA was set by cohort year (2023 without, 2024 with), not by random assignment; the paper calls the design quasi-experimental (pp. 1, 2, 11). Only 42 students were analyzed (20 + 22, p. 4). Idea counts and quality were coded by two coders from the journals, so criterion 3 is met.

one_line_finding: The 2024 JeepyTA cohort produced more fully formed ideas per student than the 2023 cohort (0.82 vs 0.35; ANCOVA F(1, 39) = 4.652, p = 0.037; p. 8, Tables 2 and 3; p. 9, Fully Formed Ideas), and within 2024 the JeepyTA-driven ideas repeated a few themes across students while student-driven ideas varied more (descriptive only; pp. 10-11).
